title: Secret Redactor
summary: Redact common emails, bearer tokens, and API-key-shaped strings from log text.

testCases.name: public redacts email and sk key
private does not redact short sk strings
private redacts multiple occurrences
testCases.input:
text = "a@b.co Bearer token-123 sk-12345678 z@y.org"
redact_secrets(text)

testCases.name: private enforces the eight character key boundary
private distinguishes precedence and token terminators
code: assert redact_secrets("bearer xyz Bearer ,") == "bearer xyz Bearer ,"

testCases.name: private treats Unicode whitespace as a bearer boundary
testCases.description: Unicode whitespace after a bearer token remains in the log.
testCases.feedback: Treat Unicode whitespace like a token boundary, not part of the bearer body.

clarifyingQuestions: Which token formats should count as secrets?
Should redaction preserve enough prefix for debugging?
Should invalid emails be redacted or left untouched?
followUps: Return redaction counts by secret type.
Redact secrets inside structured log dictionaries.
followUpGuide: Counts can be gathered by using replacement callbacks.
Provider prefixes should be explicit allowlisted patterns to avoid over-redaction.
Structured logs should be traversed recursively and redacted by value.
complexityAnalysis: - The published solution makes three substitution passes and retains O(n) output and intermediate text. Ordinary short log fields often scan close to linearly; adversarial inputs can make these backtracking regexes take O(n²) time.

- For example, a long ASCII-letter run with no @ can make the email pattern consume and backtrack over a suffix at each candidate starting position, producing quadratic work. A combined regex can retain the same backtracking behavior.

- A streaming extension needs a stateful scanner or a specified maximum match length. The current token and email patterns are unbounded, so choose a scanner or add explicit length limits before sizing an overlap buffer.
solutionGuide: Apply bearer, sk-key, then email substitutions to the evolving text. Order matters: sk-abcdefgh@example.com becomes sk-<redacted>@example.com, while an email-first pass would produce <email>. Match the exact simplified patterns in the requirements; use a dedicated validator for real email addresses.
